newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia to accept BIS membership invitation.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia to accept BIS membership invitation.

text.p: Slovenia's central bank said on Wednesday it would accept an invitation by Swiss-based Bank for International Settlements (BIS) to become a member.

Slovenian National Bank governor France Arhar said he expected the central bank council to give the go-ahead this week. The invitation, foresees Slovenia buying 10 BIS shares at a price of $12,294 each by May 30.
On Monday, BIS invited the central banks of Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Macedonia to join, leaving out the National Bank of Yugoslavia.
"This is an important step and I hope that it will help towards a solution regarding negotiations with Yugoslavia," Arhar told a news conference.
"BIS is showing Belgrade that it recognises the new central banks (of the successor republics)," he added.
The states of the former Yugoslavia, which broke up in 1991, have yet to agree on how to divide the federation's assets, held at BIS and estimated at about $660 million.
Yugoslavia has not been willing to participate in negotiations on the assets and claims it is the sole successor to the former Yugoslavia.
Voting rights attached to the 8,000 BIS shares held by the former Yugoslavia were suspended in June 1992.

BIS said it would cancel the four states' new shares when the former Yugoslav republics reached an agreement. Former Yugoslavia's suspended shares would then be divided up among them and rump Yugoslavia.

Last year BIS suggested the states split the assets according to the International Monetary Fund formula, which would give Slovenia 16.39 percent, while Croatia would get 28.49, Bosnia 13.2, Macedonia 5.4 and rump Yugoslavia 36.52 percent. Yugoslavia is alone in not supporting the BIS proposal. -- Marja Novak, Ljubljana newsroom, 386-61-125-8439
